quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Notice of Policy Changes: Leave Entitlements, Effective 1 January] The company is revising several leave entitlements following a review of employee feedback and comparable employers. Parental leave will increase from 12 to 16 weeks at full pay for either parent, with a further 8 weeks at half pay available if taken within the child's first two years. Employees must have completed at least 12 months of service to qualify for the full-pay entitlement; those with between 6 and 12 months will receive 8 weeks at full pay. Sick leave will no longer be accrued at a rate of one day per month. Instead, all employees will receive 10 days at the start of each calendar year, which may be carried forward up to a maximum of 5 days. Unused days beyond that limit will lapse on 31 December. Medical certificates will be required for absences longer than three consecutive days, an increase from the current two. Employees currently in the middle of a leave period will continue under the existing arrangements until it ends. Managers will receive guidance on applying the new rules before the end of November. Questions should be directed to the HR team, who will hold two information sessions in December.
quests.question: An employee with 9 months of service takes parental leave after 1 January. How much full-pay leave will she receive?
options: 4 weeks
8 weeks
12 weeks
16 weeks
quests.correctAnswer: 8 weeks
quests.hint: Match her length of service to the right band in the notice.
quests.explanation: She has between 6 and 12 months of service, so she receives 8 weeks at full pay.
quests.evidenceLine: those with between 6 and 12 months will receive 8 weeks at full pay

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Repair or Replace? A Practical Guide] When a smartphone breaks, the instinctive response is to buy a new one, but the better choice depends on three things: the cost of the repair, the age of the phone, and what is wrong with it. A cracked screen on a phone under three years old is usually worth repairing; an official screen replacement typically costs about a third of the price of a new mid-range model, and the rest of the phone is likely to work well for years. A failing battery is cheaper still, often under one fifth of a new phone's price, and replacing it can restore performance that has declined with age. Repairs make less sense when the phone is more than four years old and the manufacturer has stopped providing software updates, since the device may soon become insecure or incompatible with the apps you use. Water damage is a special case: even if the phone appears to work, corrosion can cause failures weeks later, so independent repairers often advise against investing heavily in it. Whatever you decide, ask for a written quote and check whether the repair is covered by a warranty.
quests.question: In which situation does the guide most clearly recommend repair?
options: A cracked screen on a phone less than three years old
An old phone that no longer receives any software updates
A water-damaged phone that seems to work normally
A phone that has no warranty left and a cracked case
quests.correctAnswer: A cracked screen on a phone less than three years old
quests.hint: Find the case described as "usually worth repairing".
quests.explanation: The guide says a cracked screen on a phone under three years old is usually worth repairing.
quests.evidenceLine: A cracked screen on a phone under three years old is usually worth repairing

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Getting to the Airport: Your Options] The airport is 28 kilometers from the city center, and there are four ways to reach it. The airport express train departs from Central Station every 15 minutes, takes 22 minutes, and costs $16 each way; tickets are cheaper, at $13, if bought online. Bus 400 takes about 55 minutes, runs every 30 minutes, and costs $5, but its last departure is at 10:30 p.m. A taxi costs between $45 and $60 depending on traffic, with the journey taking from 30 to 50 minutes; at rush hour, the lower end of the time estimate is rarely achieved. Ride-hailing services are usually 10 to 20 percent cheaper than taxis but may add a surcharge during peak demand. For travelers with early-morning flights, note that the first train leaves at 5:00 a.m. and the first bus at 4:30 a.m. Anyone arriving at the airport for an international flight should aim to be at the terminal at least two hours before departure, which means catching a train no later than the one that leaves roughly two hours and twenty-five minutes before the flight.

options: The first train would get her to the terminal in time.
The first bus would get her to the terminal in time.
Buying an online ticket would allow her to travel earlier.

quests.correctAnswer: Neither the first bus nor the first train would be early enough.
quests.hint: Work out the time she must arrive and compare it with the first departures.
quests.explanation: She needs to be at the terminal by 4:00 a.m., but the first bus leaves at 4:30 and the first train at 5:00, so neither works.

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Noise Complaints: Annual Review] The council received 2,340 noise complaints last year, up from 1,980 the year before, an increase of 18 percent. Most complaints concerned amplified music (41 percent), followed by building and construction (22 percent), barking dogs (14 percent) and vehicles (9 percent). Complaints peaked in July and August and on Friday and Saturday nights. Despite the increase, the number of formal enforcement notices fell from 210 to 176, since many complaints were resolved through mediation. The report notes that the apparent rise may partly reflect greater awareness: the council introduced an online complaint form in March, and the proportion of complaints submitted online rose from 12 percent to 47 percent. Online submissions are easier to make and record, which may have led to more complaints being logged that would previously have gone unreported. The report therefore warns against concluding that noise itself has increased by 18 percent. Residents' responses to a follow-up survey were broadly positive about the mediation service. It recommends repeating the comparison after a second full year of online reporting, and targeting patrols at the two neighborhoods that account for 35 percent of all music complaints.
quests.question: Why does the report warn against concluding that noise increased by 18 percent?
options: Complaints fell overall once the council hired inspectors.
The online form may have made complaints easier to record.
Enforcement notices rose sharply, which skews the figures.
Complaints about barking dogs disappeared entirely in March.
quests.correctAnswer: The online form may have made complaints easier to record.
quests.hint: Link the new online form to how complaints are counted.
quests.explanation: The online form made it easier to submit and record complaints, so some of the increase may be better counting rather than more noise.
quests.evidenceLine: Online submissions are easier to make and record

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Opinion: In Defense of Boredom] Parents today are anxious about their children's boredom in a way earlier generations were not. Every empty hour seems an opportunity wasted, to be filled with a lesson, a club, or a screen. Yet there is good reason to think that this anxiety is misplaced. Boredom is uncomfortable, but it is also the condition in which many children discover what they actually like. A child with nothing to do must invent something: a game, a drawing, a fort built from cushions. These activities may look trivial, but they require a child to generate ideas, make decisions, and persist without an adult's direction, skills that a scheduled life seldom provides. I am not arguing that children should be left alone for entire summers, nor that organized activities are harmful. My claim is narrower: that a child who is never allowed to be bored is also never forced to discover what to do next. A parent who answers "I'm bored" with a suggestion, a screen, or an outing has solved the child's problem, and in doing so, has quietly taken the lesson away.
quests.question: What is the writer's central claim?
options: Organized activities are harmful to children and should be avoided.
Children should be left alone for entire summers with no activities.
Boredom is always harmful to the development of children.
Some boredom helps children learn to generate their own activities.
quests.correctAnswer: Some boredom helps children learn to generate their own activities.
quests.hint: Look at the sentence that begins "My claim is narrower".
quests.explanation: The writer argues that children who are never bored never have to work out what to do next, so some boredom is useful.
quests.evidenceLine: a child who is never allowed to be bored is also never forced to discover what to do next

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Case Study: Why the Loyalty Card Failed] Daily Grind, a small café with two branches, introduced a loyalty card in January: buy nine coffees, get the tenth free. By June, the owner was disappointed. Only 14 percent of customers had signed up, and sales had not risen. When she looked at the data more closely, she found that most card holders were already regular customers who visited three or four times a week. For them, the card simply meant giving away coffee they would have bought anyway. Occasional customers, who might have been persuaded to return, rarely asked for a card, and staff did not offer it unless asked. The owner also noticed that the free coffee cost her about $1.10 in ingredients and labor, which meant that each card, once completed, reduced her margin on ten coffees by about 4 percent. She replaced the scheme with a different approach: offering a free pastry to any customer who returned within a week of their first visit, regardless of whether they held a card. By autumn, the proportion of first-time customers who came back had risen from 18 to 31 percent.
quests.question: Why did the loyalty card fail to increase sales?
options: It mainly rewarded customers who would have come anyway.
Customers disliked the coffee served at the two branches.
The card was too complicated for customers to use.
The free coffee was too small to be worth collecting.
quests.correctAnswer: It mainly rewarded customers who would have come anyway.
quests.hint: Look at who the card holders turned out to be.
quests.explanation: Most card holders were already frequent customers, so the card just gave away coffee they would have bought regardless.
quests.evidenceLine: giving away coffee they would have bought anyway

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Reading a Nutrition Label] The most common mistake people make with nutrition labels is ignoring the serving size. A label might show that a serving of breakfast cereal contains 8 grams of sugar, which seems modest, but if the serving size is 30 grams and you pour a typical 60-gram bowl, you have eaten 16 grams. The "per 100 grams" column, where it appears, is more useful for comparing products because it uses the same amount for every item. A second point is that ingredients are listed in descending order by weight, so if sugar appears first or second, it is a major component, even when the product is described as "natural". Be wary, too, of terms such as "light" or "reduced", which only mean that the product contains less of something than a comparable standard version; a "reduced-fat" item may still be high in fat, or high in sugar added to compensate. Finally, the percentages on the label, usually labeled "daily value", are based on a general reference diet and may not match your needs. They are a rough guide rather than a personal target.
quests.question: A serving is 30 grams and contains 8 grams of sugar. How much sugar is in a 60-gram portion?
options: 8 grams
12 grams
16 grams
24 grams
quests.correctAnswer: 16 grams
quests.hint: Work out how many servings are in the larger portion.
quests.explanation: A 60-gram bowl is two servings, so it contains twice the 8 grams, which is 16 grams.
quests.evidenceLine: you pour a typical 60-gram bowl, you have eaten 16 grams

quests.passage: [Reading a Nutrition Label] The most common mistake people make with nutrition labels is ignoring the serving size. A label might show that a serving of breakfast cereal contains 8 grams of sugar, which seems modest, but if the serving size is 30 grams and you pour a typical 60-gram bowl, you have eaten 16 grams. The "per 100 grams" column, where it appears, is more useful for comparing products because it uses the same amount for every item. A second point is that ingredients are listed in descending order by weight, so if sugar appears first or second, it is a major component, even when the product is described as "natural". Be wary, too, of terms such as "light" or "reduced", which only mean that the product contains less of something than a comparable standard version; a "reduced-fat" item may still be high in fat, or high in sugar added to compensate. Finally, the percentages on the label, usually labeled "daily value", are based on a general reference diet and may not match your needs. They are a rough guide rather than a personal target.
quests.question: Why is the "per 100 grams" column useful?
options: It lets you compare products on equal terms.
It shows the daily value for each person.
It lists the ingredients by weight.
It is always more accurate than the serving column.
quests.correctAnswer: It lets you compare products on equal terms.
quests.hint: Think about what happens when two products have different serving sizes.
quests.explanation: Because every product is measured per 100 grams, shoppers can compare like with like.
quests.evidenceLine: it uses the same amount for every item

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Why There Are Two High Tides a Day] Most people learn that the moon's gravity pulls the oceans toward it, which explains one high tide each day on the side of the Earth facing the moon. The puzzle is why there is a second high tide on the opposite side. The explanation lies in the fact that gravity weakens with distance. The moon pulls the near side of the Earth more strongly than its center, and the center more strongly than the far side. The differences in pull stretch the oceans in two directions at once: toward the moon on the near side, and away from it on the far side, where the water is pulled least and is, in effect, left behind. As the Earth rotates, any given coastline passes through both bulges each day, which is why most coasts experience two high tides roughly twelve and a half hours apart. The sun also exerts a tidal pull, about 46 percent as strong as the moon's despite its much greater mass, because it is so much farther away. When the sun and moon line up, at new and full moon, their effects combine to produce unusually high "spring" tides; when they pull at right angles, tides are weaker.
quests.question: Why does a second high tide occur on the side of the Earth facing away from the moon?
options: The moon's gravity is strongest on the far side of the Earth.
The far side is pulled least, so the water is effectively left behind.
The sun pushes the water toward that side of the planet during the day.
The Earth stops rotating for a moment and the water piles up.
quests.correctAnswer: The far side is pulled least, so the water is effectively left behind.
quests.hint: Think about how the strength of the pull changes from the near side to the far side.
quests.explanation: The far side is pulled least, so the water there bulges away from the moon relative to the rest of the Earth.
quests.evidenceLine: where the water is pulled least and is, in effect, left behind

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Course Policy: Use of AI Writing Tools] Students may use AI writing tools in this course under the following conditions. Tools may be used to brainstorm ideas, check grammar and clarify explanations, provided that students then write their own text. Submitting text generated by an AI tool as your own work, in whole or in part, is considered academic misconduct. Any use of an AI tool must be acknowledged in a short note at the end of the assignment, stating which tool was used and for what purpose. Students are responsible for checking the accuracy of any information obtained through such tools, since these systems can produce statements that sound plausible but are false; an error that originates in a tool's output will not be accepted as an excuse. For in-class tests, no electronic tools of any kind are permitted. If you are unsure whether a particular use is permitted, ask the instructor before submitting the work, not afterward. The instructor may ask you to explain or discuss your work in person to confirm that it reflects your own understanding. Penalties for misconduct range from a zero on the assignment to referral to the faculty disciplinary committee, depending on the seriousness of the case and whether it is a first offense.
quests.question: Which use of an AI tool is permitted under the policy?
options: Having the tool write a paragraph that the student then lightly edits
Using the tool quietly during an in-class test to check answers
Checking the grammar of text the student wrote, and acknowledging it
Submitting the tool's summary as part of the essay without mentioning it
quests.correctAnswer: Checking the grammar of text the student wrote, and acknowledging it
quests.hint: Compare each option with both the permitted uses and the acknowledgment rule.
quests.explanation: Grammar checking is allowed if students write their own text, and any use must be acknowledged in a note.
quests.evidenceLine: check grammar and clarify explanations

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [The Quiet Return of Paper Maps] Sales of printed maps have risen for several years in a row, which would have surprised anyone who predicted that smartphones would end them. Retailers report that the buyers are not nostalgic collectors but hikers, cyclists and drivers who have discovered the limits of their phones: batteries die, signals fail in valleys, and a small screen shows only a narrow slice of the landscape. A paper map shows everything at once. This is the point that map enthusiasts stress most. Planning a route on a screen means zooming in and out and holding the relationship between places in your head; on paper, the relationships are simply visible. Some researchers have suggested that people who navigate with maps form better mental representations of an area than those who follow turn-by-turn directions, though the evidence is still limited and the studies small. It would be a mistake to turn this into a campaign against technology. Most paper-map users also carry a phone, and many use both: the map to understand the territory, the phone to find the exact spot where they are standing. What the revival shows is not that one tool is better, but that each answers a different question.
quests.question: According to the passage, who is buying printed maps?
options: Mostly nostalgic collectors of old printed maps
People who have found the limits of phone navigation
Mainly tourists who are visiting large cities abroad
Mainly teachers and students who study geography
quests.correctAnswer: People who have found the limits of phone navigation
quests.hint: Look at the contrast introduced by "not ... but".
quests.explanation: Retailers say buyers are hikers, cyclists and drivers who discovered what phones cannot do, not collectors.
quests.evidenceLine: not nostalgic collectors but hikers, cyclists and drivers
